```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE, comment="#>", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE,
  fig.width=9, fig.height=4.2, dpi=160)
```

L0glm's shrinking active set, compiled solvers and fast GIC preset can deliver
striking gains in both speed and support recovery. These examples compare
complete fitting and selection workflows, with the tuning rule stated for every
method. The tables are generated by the
[repository's reproducible README benchmark](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/L0glm/blob/master/README.Rmd).

## One million predictors

The design has 500 observations, one million standard-normal predictors and
60 nonzero coefficients of either sign. L0glm uses GIC-preset ISIS plus a relaxed
refit. LASSO and fully relaxed LASSO are tuned by BIC or five-fold CV.

| Method | Selection | Seconds | GIC | TP | FP | FN | TN | F1 | MCC |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **L0glm + ISIS** | GIC preset | **3.16** | **2583** | **40** | **3** | 20 | 999937 | **0.777** | **0.787** |
| LASSO | BIC path | 22.75 | 14789 | 23 | 612 | 37 | 999328 | 0.066 | 0.118 |
| Relaxed LASSO | BIC path | 21.42 | 10588 | 21 | 453 | 39 | 999487 | 0.079 | 0.124 |
| LASSO | 5-fold CV | 123.13 | 4309 | 17 | 50 | 43 | 999890 | 0.268 | 0.268 |
| Relaxed LASSO | 5-fold CV | 91.76 | 7413 | 20 | 252 | 40 | 999688 | 0.120 | 0.156 |

```{r million-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Complete-workflow timings and false positives in the million-predictor example. L0glm uses a GIC preset; both LASSO methods use five-fold CV."}
par(mfrow=c(1, 2), mar=c(4, 8.2, 2, 1), mgp=c(2.5, .6, 0), family="sans",
  bg="white", col.axis="#34465d", col.lab="#34465d", col.main="#0a1930")
labels <- c("L0glm + ISIS", "LASSO", "Relaxed LASSO")
cols <- c("#087e83", "#8b5cc7", "#d04a78")
seconds <- c(3.16, 123.13, 91.76)
plot(seconds, 3:1, log="x", xlim=c(1, 220), ylim=c(.6, 3.4), pch=21, bg=cols,
  col=cols, cex=2.2, yaxt="n", xlab="Seconds (log scale)", ylab="", bty="n")
axis(2, at=3:1, labels=labels, las=1, tick=FALSE, cex.axis=.9)
abline(v=c(1, 10, 100), col="#e1ebef", lty=3)
points(seconds, 3:1, pch=21, bg=cols, col=cols, cex=2.2)
text(seconds, 3:1, sprintf("%.2f s", seconds), pos=ifelse(seconds > 50, 2, 4),
  offset=.8, cex=.8, col="#29455a")
title("Fast fitting and selection", adj=0, cex.main=1.1)
fp <- c(3, 50, 252)
plot(fp, 3:1, xlim=c(0, 310), ylim=c(.6, 3.4), pch=21, bg=cols, col=cols,
  cex=2.2, yaxt="n", xlab="False positives", ylab="", bty="n")
axis(2, at=3:1, labels=labels, las=1, tick=FALSE, cex.axis=.9)
text(fp+9, 3:1, fp, pos=4, cex=.9, col="#29455a")
title("A cleaner selected support", adj=0, cex.main=1.1)
```

In this simulation L0glm is **39 times faster than five-fold-CV LASSO** and
recovers more true effects with fewer false positives. The L0glm timing includes
screening and one preset fit; the other methods evaluate up to 40 native path
values, with paths refitted in each CV training fold. BIC is shown alongside CV
because GIC can select a null LASSO model at this dimension. All rows retain GIC
as a common evaluation score. Five-fold comparisons use the same random folds.

Simulation is excluded from timings. The documented run uses one BLAS thread
and eight screening threads; the design is held in memory. See the
[million-predictor tutorial](high-dimensional.html) for the complete data setup.

## Single-channel deconvolution

A 500-predictor blurred Poisson spike train contains 50 events. All fitted
models are scored using the original Poisson likelihood and GIC.

| Method | Seconds | GIC | TP | FP | FN | TN | F1 | MCC |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **L0glm** | **0.06** | **4824** | 43 | **5** | 7 | 445 | **0.878** | **0.864** |
| ABESS | 1.14 | 7616 | 31 | 16 | 19 | 434 | 0.639 | 0.601 |
| LASSO | 0.28 | 6001 | 48 | 88 | 2 | 362 | 0.516 | 0.515 |
| Relaxed LASSO | 0.16 | 5323 | 45 | 31 | 5 | 419 | 0.714 | 0.694 |

L0glm uses one GIC preset; glmnet searches ten lambda values. ABESS searches
integer support sizes with warm starts. For identity-link Poisson data,
alternative backends use explicitly labelled weighted-Gaussian approximations;
L0glm fits the Poisson likelihood directly.

## Multichannel deconvolution

The grouped example contains 25 active predictor rows. Spectra are sparse within
rows. Row metrics measure event recovery; within-row metrics are calculated
among correctly recovered true-positive rows.

| Method | Seconds | GIC | TP | FP | FN | Row F1 | Row MCC | Within-row F1 | Within-row MCC |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **L0glm** | **0.48** | **118549** | **25** | **0** | **0** | **1.000** | **1.000** | **0.946** | **0.913** |
| ABESS | 2.00 | 127603 | 22 | 3 | 3 | 0.880 | 0.874 | 0.846 | 0.763 |
| LASSO | 3.73 | 130115 | 24 | 11 | 1 | 0.800 | 0.800 | 0.863 | 0.789 |
| Relaxed LASSO | 21.63 | 122388 | 25 | 1 | 0 | 0.980 | 0.980 | 0.880 | 0.809 |

L0glm recovers every event row without false positives in this example, and also
gives the strongest within-row sparsity recovery. Grouped Gaussian approximations
use shared observation-row weights, while L0glm uses channel-specific Poisson
working weights. The [deconvolution tutorial](deconvolution.html) shows the signal,
coefficient and heatmap comparisons with every simulated channel retained.

## Native validation and OpenMP

Native validation scoring preserves multichannel OpenMP and returns the same
checkpoint models as the R-validation path. This reproducible test uses
1,000 predictors, 16 channels, 60 active rows and an independent Poisson replicate
for validation. Median times are from five fits, with one BLAS thread.

| Backend | Outcome threads | Seconds | Validation deviance | GIC | F1 | MCC |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| General R | 1 | 1.12 | 0.357612 | 42728.05 | 0.944882 | 0.942790 |
| Native | 1 | 0.08 | 0.357612 | 42728.05 | 0.944882 | 0.942790 |
| Native | 2 | 0.06 | 0.357612 | 42728.05 | 0.944882 | 0.942790 |
| Native | 4 | 0.04 | 0.357612 | 42728.05 | 0.944882 | 0.942790 |
| Native | 8 | 0.04 | 0.357612 | 42728.05 | 0.944882 | 0.942790 |

Run [benchmark_native_validation.R](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/L0glm/blob/master/benchmarks/benchmark_native_validation.R)
to reproduce this comparison. Results agree across thread counts; validation
predictors are shared across workers. Paired 10,000-predictor tests also preserve
the unvalidated fit, with 16-channel timing 0.874 s versus 0.878 s.

## Reproduce and extend

* [README benchmark source](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/L0glm/blob/master/README.Rmd): data generation, comparisons and plots.
* [Solver/problem-size benchmark](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/L0glm/blob/master/benchmarks/1_benchmarks_L0glm_solvers_problem_sizes.R): solvers, families, matrix storage and sizes.
* [Single/multichannel benchmark](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/L0glm/blob/master/benchmarks/2_benchmarks_L0glm_single_and_multichannel_vs_other_methods.R): detailed signal examples and alternative methods.
* [`sparseglm()`](../reference/sparseglm.html): use the same comparison framework on your own data.

Timings measure complete workflows on a Windows workstation with OpenBLAS and
will vary with hardware and tuning choices. F1 and MCC evaluate the known simulated
support; it is never used to select models. Likelihood floors and approximation
labels are explicit in the benchmark source.
